content_voiceover: This diagram walks through the mechanics of the direct and indirect antiglobulin tests, and you need to be crystal clear on what each one actually detects. The direct antiglobulin test, or direct Coombs test, starts with the patient's own red cells, which already have autoantibody bound to them in vivo. You wash the cells, then add anti-human globulin, or AHG, reagent, which is itself an antibody against human IgG or complement. The AHG reagent bridges the antibody-coated red cells together, causing visible agglutination, a positive direct Coombs test therefore tells you the patient's own red cells are coated with antibody or complement in vivo, this is the test you order first when you suspect AIHA. The indirect antiglobulin test works in the opposite direction, you take the patient's serum, which may contain free antibodies, and mix it with reagent red cells of known antigen phenotype. If the serum antibodies bind the reagent cells, adding AHG again causes agglutination. The indirect test detects antibodies circulating in the serum or plasma, or antibodies eluted off a patient's red cells, that's the eluate technique, and this is the test used for antibody screening before transfusion and for identifying antibody specificity in AIHA workups. The key distinction for boards, direct tests the patient's cells, indirect tests the patient's serum or an eluate.
keypoints: DAT (direct Coombs): tests patient RBCs for in-vivo bound Ab/complement, AHG causes agglutination if positive
IAT (indirect Coombs): tests patient serum + reagent RBCs for free circulating antibody
IAT also used to test eluate (antibody stripped off patient RBCs)
AHG reagent = antibody against human IgG/complement, bridges coated RBCs to agglutinate
DAT positive = order first when AIHA suspected; IAT = pretransfusion antibody screen/ID
keypoint_voiceover: Direct versus indirect antiglobulin test, keep the direction straight. The direct test, or direct Coombs, uses the patient's own red cells, which already carry antibody or complement in vivo, adding anti-human globulin reagent causes agglutination if positive, this is your first test when you suspect AIHA. The indirect test uses patient serum mixed with reagent red cells, detecting free antibody in the serum, or it can test an eluate, antibody stripped off the patient's own cells, and this is the workhorse for pretransfusion antibody screening and specificity identification. Bottom line, direct tests the cells, indirect tests the serum or the eluate.
